summary:
Astronauts rarely get the sleep they need. On the International Space Station, a crew member sees sixteen sunrises in a single day, and the natural cycle that tells the body when to sleep is thrown off. NASA’s Human Research Program has reported sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload in flight crews, and has called for tools to assess each astronaut’s individual sleep need. Melatonin, the hormone that signals sleep, has been tried in space, but as a fixed dose, even though people process it differently depending on factors such as age, weight and height.

Team AquaCat’s answer is Astromnia, a health monitoring system built on one idea: measure first, then dose. The astronaut provides one drop of saliva, with no needles and no laboratory. A screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE) biosensor reacts to the melatonin in the sample. A mini potentiostat, small enough to connect to a phone, applies differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) and records the peak current produced.


The system has four main strengths. It is personal, because each astronaut’s own result replaces a one-size-fits-all pill. It is portable, needing only a phone, a compact reader and a disposable sensor strip. It is non-invasive, since it uses saliva rather than blood. It also supports mission readiness, because better-managed sleep protects performance, safety and long-term health.
details:
Astronauts live with disrupted light-dark cycles, irregular schedules and stress. These disturb the circadian rhythm and sleep, which affect health, alertness and performance. Melatonin is the key hormone that regulates sleep, but there is no simple way to measure it in space and personalized its dosage.

Melatonin is usually given as a standard dose, without knowing an individual's actual melatonin level. Astronauts need a compact, low-resource and non-invasive way to monitor melatonin so supplementation can be matched to the individual.

Our Solution

Astromnia measures melatonin first, then guides the dose.

A saliva sensor: a small screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE) carrying a melatonin-binding DNA aptamer.

A mini potentiostat: a pocket-sized circuit that connects to a smartphone and reads the sensor.

A software (Astromnia): turns the reading into a melatonin level and suggests a personalised dose.

How It Works

  1. The astronaut mixes a small saliva sample with a binding buffer in a tube and dips the sensor into the mixture.
  2. The mini potentiostat runs a measurement called differential pulse voltammetry (DPV). When melatonin binds the aptamer on the electrode, the electrode's DPV signal changes, and the size of the change depends on how much melatonin is present.
  3. The software converts the signal change into a melatonin concentration using a calibration line.
  4. The software checks the result against the limit of quantification (LOQ), the lowest level the sensor can measure reliably. Readings below it are not used.
  5. The software compares the level with a reference range for the time of day and suggests a dosage and timing.

Use Across a Mission

Before: record each astronaut's baseline melatonin profile and plan their sleep schedule.

During: track changes caused by microgravity and altered light cycles, and adjust the dose.

After: support readjustment to Earth's day-night cycle.

Why It Is Different

  1. Non-invasive: saliva needs no needles or blood.
  2. Compact: a disposable strip, a small circuit and a phone suit limited space and power.
  3. Personal: the dose is based on the astronaut's own level, not a standard pill.
  4. Complete: it goes from measurement to a dosage decision in one system.
  5. NASA has studied astronaut sleep and melatonin, and a NASA-partly-funded test at Washington State University measures melatonin from blood with a phone reader. Astromnia uses saliva and an electrochemical sensor, and adds the dosage software.

Feasibility

  • The sensor, circuit and software use proven techniques: electrochemical sensing, a small potentiostat and a calibration line.
  • The software needs only peak detection, a linear calibration and a rule-based dose comparison, which run on a standard phone.
  • Dose rules will be set with a medical advisor. The system supports decisions and does not replace flight surgeons.

Proposed measurement workflow

  1. Tube with buffer. A tube is supplied prefilled with binding buffer.
  2. Add saliva. The astronaut adds saliva up to the fill line.
  3. Cap and shake. The tube is capped and shaken well to mix saliva and buffer thoroughly.
  4. Open, dip and detect. The tube is opened and the sensing end of the strip is dipped into the mixture, with the electrical contacts kept dry. The portable potentiostat runs the DPV measurement and sends the result to the phone.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

  • Image: Generated the illustrated scenes using ChatGPT.
  • Video: When assembling the scenes into a short introduction video, we used HeyGen (through Claude plugins) to generate and produce the video.
  • Voiceover: When we needed narration for the video, we used Fish Audio to turn our written script into a voiceover.
  • Script and Written Materials: When drafting and refining the narration script, subtitles, project summary, video description and this declaration, we used Claude (Anthropic) for writing suggestions and wording.
  • Coding (Implementation Guidance): When uncertain about how to implement specific features of the Astromnia app, we prompted ChatGPT and Claude for coding suggestions and design best practices.
  • Coding (Debugging Assistance): During development, ChatGPT and Claude were used to help identify, explain and resolve coding errors.
